newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Proposed amnesty stirs protests in Guatemala.
newsitem.headline: Proposed amnesty stirs protests in Guatemala.

text.p: Human rights activists protested in Guatemala's Congress on Monday against an amnesty proposal that could let people responsible for massacres go unpunished.

The amnesty has been proposed as part of a peace agreement ending a 36-year civil war, but rights advocates fear army officers accused of ordering the murder of opponents and intellectuals would never stand trial.

About 75 demonstrators carrying black banners interrupted legislators as they debated a bill that would grant limited amnesty to guerrilla fighters and members of the armed forces accused of war crimes.
"We insist that they don't pass any law that promotes impunity in Guatemala," Miguel Angel Albizures, spokesman for the Alliance Against Impunity, told reporters at the rally.

"Under this law if they murdered someone to suppress a political crime that goes unpunished. If they kidnapped someone because they believed that person collaborated with the guerrillas, that goes unpunished," he said.

In Madrid last week, Guatemalan government negotiators and guerrilla representatives signed an agreement that defined the terms for an amnesty for guerrilla fighters and military personnel who committed crimes connected to the civil war.
The accord was the final step to a definitive peace treaty scheduled to be signed in Guatemala City on Dec. 29, which will end Central America's longest civil war.
As the rights activists staged their protest in Congress, business leaders announced their support for the amnesty.
"This accord makes peace feasible in this country," said Chamber of Commerce president Jorge Briz at a news conference.
He said the amnesty did not cover serious crimes such as the kidnapping and murder of civilians during the armed leftist revolt and the army's counterinsurgency campaigns.
